title: How U.S. Allies Can Resist Washington's Bullying
gist: The Trump administration's ICC sanctions campaign relies on 'surrogate enforcers' (foreign banks, cloud providers, insurers) over-complying to avoid U.S. dollar-system risk, and the authors argue U.S. allies could blunt this coercive leverage with EU-style blocking statutes, non-dollar payment rails, and collective sanction-protection mechanisms, using the ICC as a low-cost test case.

themes.theme: Mechanics of U.S. extraterritorial sanctions power

insights.claim: The U.S. sanctioned 13 ICC staff members including nine judges over the Rome Statute-based Palestine investigation; former chief prosecutor Karim Khan lost email and bank access, and judge Kimberly Prost lost her credit cards and had Amazon devices stop functioning, showing how personal sanctions cascade into everyday commercial services.
insights.speaker: Mieczyslaw P. Boduszynski, Christopher K. Lamont
insights.so_what: Illustrates how modern U.S. sanctions bite through consumer/commercial tech and finance dependencies rather than direct asset freezes alone, a template applicable to any future sanctions target reliant on U.S.-linked services.
insights.locator: One striking example of Washington's coercive diplomacy

insights.claim: The U.S. cannot formally compel ICC states like Japan, Germany, or France to abandon the Rome Statute since Washington isn't a party, contributes nothing to the ICC budget, and has no vote in the Assembly of States Parties — the leverage instead comes from threatening the banks and companies of allied nations with U.S. sanctions exposure.
insights.speaker: Mieczyslaw P. Boduszynski, Christopher K. Lamont
insights.so_what: Reframes U.S. sanctions power as dependent on private-sector 'surrogate enforcers' rather than formal treaty leverage — meaning allied governments retain more latitude to intervene at the corporate compliance layer than diplomatic rhetoric suggests.
insights.quote: Rubio does not need parties to the Rome Statute— such as Japan, Germany, or France—to formally sign on to his campaign to dismantle the ICC. But he does need their banks and companies to fear U.S. sanctions.
insights.locator: One striking example of Washington's coercive diplomacy

insights.claim: Risk-averse foreign banks and companies systematically over-comply with U.S. sanctions rather than risk their U.S. market access, dollar clearing, or investor relationships — a behavior reinforced by the memory of the nearly $9 billion penalty imposed on France's BNP Paribas in 2014 for routing prohibited transactions through the U.S. financial system.
insights.speaker: Mieczyslaw P. Boduszynski, Christopher K. Lamont
insights.so_what: The BNP Paribas precedent functions as a durable deterrent multiplier — a single historical enforcement action continues to shape global bank compliance behavior over a decade later, meaning U.S. sanctions reach far beyond what formal jurisdiction alone would predict.

insights.claim: The U.S. dollar accounted for 89.2% of all foreign exchange trades in April 2025 and roughly 57% of disclosed global reserves in Q1 2026, while over half of international banking claims and liabilities are dollar-denominated — underpinning why dollar-system exposure is the chokepoint Washington uses for coercive leverage.
insights.speaker: Mieczyslaw P. Boduszynski, Christopher K. Lamont
insights.so_what: Quantifies the structural basis of dollar hegemony that underlies U.S. sanctions reach; any de-dollarization trend (euro payment systems, non-dollar reserve diversification) directly erodes this coercive tool over time.
insights.locator: Washington's reach rests on the central role

insights.claim: Three U.S. firms — Amazon, Microsoft, and Google — provide roughly two-thirds of the European Union's cloud services, and as of 2024, Amazon Web Services alone accounted for 97% of deployed systems on Japan's government cloud.
insights.speaker: Mieczyslaw P. Boduszynski, Christopher K. Lamont
insights.so_what: Cloud infrastructure concentration in three U.S. hyperscalers is a geopolitical vulnerability for U.S. allies, reinforcing the long-term investment case for sovereign/European cloud alternatives as a policy and market priority.
insights.quote: As late as 2024, Amazon Web Services alone accounted for 97 percent of deployed systems on Japan's government cloud.
insights.locator: Washington's reach rests on the central role

themes.theme: Precedent: the Greenland episode as proof allies can push back

insights.claim: Trump's threats to annex Greenland prompted European governments to rally behind Denmark, prepare a retaliatory tariff package worth 93 billion euros, consider invoking the EU's Anti-Coercion Instrument, and see the European Parliament suspend work on a U.S.-EU trade agreement — after which Trump withdrew the tariff threat within four days.
insights.speaker: Mieczyslaw P. Boduszynski, Christopher K. Lamont
insights.so_what: Concrete proof-of-concept that coordinated allied economic retaliation with credible teeth can force a rapid U.S. climbdown — a template the authors argue should be replicated for the ICC and other coercion episodes.
insights.quote: Trump ultimately withdrew the tariff threat four days after announcing it, showing that a coordinated response with credible economic consequences can raise the costs of coercion and alter Washington's calculations.

insights.claim: Shielding an entire economy from U.S. sanctions is likely unrealistic — as Brussels found when it tried to protect EU-Iran trade in 2018 — but protecting a narrow set of identifiable individuals and institutions (like ICC officials) is a more feasible, bounded goal.
insights.speaker: Mieczyslaw P. Boduszynski, Christopher K. Lamont
insights.so_what: Distinguishes between two very different scales of anti-coercion strategy: broad economy-wide sanctions-shielding (largely failed historically) versus narrow, targeted protection of specific actors (more tractable) — a useful framework for assessing future EU/allied sanctions-evasion efforts.

themes.theme: Proposed allied countermeasures and their limits

insights.claim: The authors propose that the EU, UK, Japan, Canada, Australia, South Korea, Norway, and Switzerland form a standing consultation and mutual-support mechanism to rapidly coordinate legal/diplomatic responses and cost-sharing whenever a member or a rules-based institution faces U.S. coercion.
insights.speaker: Mieczyslaw P. Boduszynski, Christopher K. Lamont
insights.so_what: A proposed multilateral 'anti-coercion coalition' would be a structural check on U.S. secondary sanctions leverage — worth tracking as an emerging institutional trend that could reduce the effectiveness of future U.S. sanctions campaigns against allies.
insights.locator: As a first order of business

insights.claim: The EU's existing Blocking Statute (countering extraterritorial sanctions effects) has seen uneven enforcement left to member states and hasn't eliminated the underlying commercial asymmetry, since firms still choose to comply with Washington over risking loss of U.S. market access.
insights.speaker: Mieczyslaw P. Boduszynski, Christopher K. Lamont
insights.so_what: Existing EU legal tools against U.S. extraterritorial sanctions have proven weak in practice, meaning any effective pushback requires new enforcement teeth, not just existing statutes.
insights.quote: Faced with uneven or uncertain penalties in Europe and the possible loss of the U.S. market, most large companies still choose Washington.
insights.locator: The European Union already has a Blocking Statute

insights.claim: The authors recommend concrete non-dollar infrastructure for protected individuals/institutions: a publicly backed bank or payment provider operating in euros, yen, or pounds without U.S. correspondent accounts, locally controlled email/cloud services, and an emergency legal-defense fund.
insights.speaker: Mieczyslaw P. Boduszynski, Christopher K. Lamont
insights.so_what: A concrete blueprint for 'de-dollarized' payment and cloud infrastructure targeted at insulating specific institutions — a narrow but real driver of demand for non-U.S. financial and cloud infrastructure providers.

insights.claim: Resistance carries real risks: Washington could escalate against a protected bank, impose tariffs, restrict intelligence sharing, or exploit disagreements among allies, while China and Russia could exploit any resulting rupture, and defanged U.S. sanctions could also benefit genuine bad actors who make up the majority of sanctioned individuals.
insights.speaker: Mieczyslaw P. Boduszynski, Christopher K. Lamont
insights.so_what: A balanced acknowledgment that anti-coercion strategies carry blowback risk, tempering the thesis and suggesting incremental rather than wholesale allied de-dollarization/de-risking is the realistic path.
insights.locator: To be sure, such resistance carries risks

source_meta.author: Mieczyslaw P. Boduszynski, Christopher K. Lamont
